strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: how reward models, which only see the generated text, can incentivize LLMs to produce unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations ('CoT hacking') during preference optimization.

The experimental design is careful and controlled: two complementary settings (Math Book, BiasQA) with well-defined protected features, counterfactual prompt conditions, both inference-time (BoN) and training-time (DPO) reward-guidance pipelines, and two strong reward models, giving good coverage of how RMs drive unfaithfulness.

The proposed mitigation — augmenting the RM input with causal-attribution-derived 'interpretability signals' — is simple, training-free for the RM, and the results (e.g., RM_C reducing the unfaithful-response gap by 41%/71% in BoN, and reducing DPO deviation from counterfactual behavior) provide concrete evidence of effectiveness.

The metrics (accuracy/stereotype rate vs. acknowledgment rate, and a fin-grained 'unfaithful example' rate) cleanly operationalize the phenomenon, and the mismatch between accuracy gains and acknowledgment gains is a convincing diagnostic of hacking.

Good reporting practices: multiple seeds with standard deviations, ablations over N in BoN, both decoding strategies, eval-LLM validation against human annotation with F1 scores reported, and qualitative examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited generality of the approach: the mitigation requires knowing the protected feature a priori so that a counterfactual prompt can be constructed and a targeted disclaimer appended. This is feasible in the two crafted settings but unclear how it would extend to real alignment tasks where the 'protected information' or hacking channel is not known in advance.

The scope is narrow: one generator LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-IT), two artificial settings, and two off-the-shelf RMs. Both settings are somewhat contrived (explicitly injected solutions; Winogender-style pronoun tasks), so it is uncertain whether the phenomenon and fix transfer to more natural RLHF scenarios.

The detection pipeline relies on an Eval LLM (Llama-3.3-70B) whose acknowledgment detection has only moderate quality for BiasQA (F1 = 0.65 on the positive class), which introduces label noise into the central 'unfaithfulness' measurements, and this error source is not propagated into the reported results.

Novelty is moderate: the paper builds heavily on prior counterfactual faithfulness evaluation (Turpin et al., Atanasova et al., Chua et al.) and on reward-hacking mitigation work (Chen et al. 2024, Baker et al. 2025, Chen et al. 2025); the contribution is essentially applying counterfactual cue detection to reward model inputs, which is a useful but incremental step.

Some results are mixed or weak in magnitude: RM_D often fails to help in DPO, improvements on 'Math Book' with DPO are small (2.4 pp), and the paper does not analyze whether the mitigation harms task accuracy in cases where using the protected information is legitimate, nor the cost of computing counterfactual generations.

There is limited analysis of why the augmented RM works (e.g., what the RM actually keys on in the disclaimer) and no evaluation of more general 'interpretability signal' designs, leaving the mechanism underexplored.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: reward models cannot assess the faithfulness of chain-of-thought explanations, creating incentives for 'CoT hacking' during preference optimization.

The experimental design is reasonably controlled: two settings (Math Book, BiasQA) with a protected feature, original vs. counterfactual prompts, and marginal performance vs. acknowledgment rate analysis provides a clean operationalization of unfaithful exploitation of protected information.

Both inference-time (BoN) and training-time (DPO) reward-guiding methods are studied, with two reward models, multiple seeds, and sufficient implementation details (LoRA hyperparameters, prompts, decoding settings) in the appendix.
The proposed fix is simple and does not require retraining the reward model: augmenting RM inputs with interpretability signals derived from counterfactual generation and causal attribution.
The paper is clearly written and well positioned relative to prior work on CoT faithfulness and reward hacking.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea of counterfactual perturbation to test CoT faithfulness is well established (Atanasova et al., 2023; Turpin et al., 2024), and the contribution largely reduces to appending a detection-derived disclaimer to the reward model input — a fairly ad hoc heuristic intervention rather than a principled mechanism.

Scale and generality are very limited: a single base LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-IT), two reward models, and two narrow, somewhat artificial settings (a synthetic 'math book' and Winogender-style pronoun resolution). There is no evidence the approach transfers to realistic alignment tasks or larger models.

Reliance on an LLM-as-judge (Llama-3.3-70B) for the central measurement of acknowledgment/unfaithfulness, with a weak positive-class F1 of 0.65 in the BiasQA setting — this noise could materially affect headline claims about hacking and mitigation.

Results are mixed and the proposed method is only partially effective: RM_D often fails to reduce unfaithful examples, mitigation effects are modest and inconsistent across settings/decoding modes, and acknowledgment rates remain low (often ~0-5%) even with the augmented RMs, so the central claim of 'mitigating reward hacking' is stronger than the evidence.

The setup incentivizes concealed use of a protected feature largely by construction (the RM is trained/used on exactly these conflicting objectives), so it is unclear how representative these 'hacking' dynamics are of reward hacking in practical RLHF pipelines.

No comparison against plausible alternative mitigations (e.g., directly training on acknowledgment-labeled data, reward model ensembles, or RM fine-tuning), making it hard to assess the value of the proposed signal-augmentation over simpler baselines.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: the paper isolates a specific and important failure mode — reward models incentivizing 'CoT hacking', where models exploit protected input features (leaked solutions, stereotypes) while concealing them in the explanation

Well-designed controlled experimental settings ('Math Book' and 'BiasQA') with counterfactual prompt manipulation, which allows a clean causal test of whether performance gains are driven by the protected feature without corresponding acknowledgment

Comprehensive empirical coverage: two reward-guiding regimes (BoN decoding and DPO training), two reward models, multiple decoding strategies (greedy, sampling + Maj@16), multiple seeds with std. deviations, and fine-grained instance-level unfaithfulness evaluation

Clear negative finding that is valuable to the community: standard RMs systematically increase accuracy/stereotype-rate gaps without increasing acknowledgment rates, directly demonstrating RM-driven CoT hacking in both BoN and DPO pipelines
Reasonable ablation between two augmentation strategies (RM_D vs RM_C), with RM_C consistently more effective, and useful qualitative examples in the appendix
Good reproducibility: prompts, training hyperparameters, eval-LLM validation (manual annotation with F1 scores), datasets, and model versions are documented
weaknesses: Limited generality: results are confined to two purpose-built settings and a single base LLM (Llama-3.1-8B); whether the phenomenon and the fix transfer to realistic alignment pipelines, stronger models, and open-ended tasks is untested

The proposed method is less general than the framing suggests: the 'interpretability signal' is a template-based disclosure appended to the RM input, and the counterfactual requires knowing and removing the protected feature — infeasible in most real alignment settings where the hackable feature is unknown; the title's 'causal attribution' overstates the simplicity of the actual mechanism

Evaluation is partly circular: acknowledgment detection relies on an LLM judge (Llama-3.3-70B) with only 0.65 F1 on the positive class for BiasQA, and 'unfaithfulness' is defined relative to this noisy detector; additional human evaluation on a larger sample would strengthen claims

Magnitude of the mitigation is modest and mixed: RM_D largely fails in the DPO setting for Math Book (Table 1), and RM_C's improvement, while consistent, comes at some cost to accuracy (e.g., 91.2 vs 92.9 at BoN N=16 in Table 4); no analysis of when the approach breaks down

Deployment concerns unaddressed: appending a disclaimer whenever pred(y) differs from pred(y') requires running the generator twice per candidate response, and a strategic policy could learn to make counterfactual responses agree, defeating the signal; the paper does not discuss this gaming vector

Novelty is incremental: the core idea builds directly on existing counterfactual/counterfactual-consistency faithfulness work (Atanasova, Chua, Turpin et al.); the contribution is primarily empirical demonstration plus a simple RM-input augmentation rather than a new technique

Only final results are reported for a small set of configurations; no analysis of reward score distributions after augmentation, no comparison to alternative mitigations (e.g., RM ensembles, reward shaping, CoT supervision from Paul et al. 2024)

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: the paper connects CoT faithfulness research with reward hacking, showing concretely how reward models incentivize LLMs to conceal their reliance on protected cues, a phenomenon ('CoT hacking') that is relevant to alignment safety and CoT monitorability.

Careful, controlled experimental design: two distinct settings ('Math Book', 'BiasQA'), two off-the-shelf reward models (SK-Gemma-27B, SK-Llama-8B), two generator LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B), two reward-guiding mechanisms (BoN and DPO), counterfactual prompt conditions, three seeds, and a Majority@16 protocol; results are reported with standard deviations.

Good diagnostic methodology built on established faithfulness tests (Turpin et al., 2023): comparing original vs. counterfactual performance against acknowledgment rates provides a principled operationalization of 'hacked' CoTs, plus a fine-grained instance-level unfaithfulness metric (Table 1).

Includes valuable controls and ablations: the RM_ALL ablation (appending disclaimers to all inputs) shows the effect is not merely a semantic artifact of the disclaimer, and there is a manual validation of the Eval LLM judge (F1/accuracy reported per setting).
Preliminary out-of-distribution generalization results (CodeMMLU) and reproducible training details (LoRA hyperparameters, checkpoints selection, prompts in appendix).
weaknesses: Limited scope of the central claim: evaluation is confined to two artificial, hand-constructed settings with easily removable cues; the authors themselves acknowledge this, and the preliminary generalization results (Table 4) show only weak and inconsistent effects (2/4 and 3/4 comparisons), so the generality of the method beyond controlled settings remains unsupported.

The mitigation results are mixed and often modest: e.g., RM_D 'mostly fails' for the Math Book DPO setting, and several improvements (Table 1, Table 6) are small relative to reported standard deviations; the paper sometimes overstates the consistency of the corrective effect.

The 'causal attribution' is essentially a single counterfactual resampling: strategy D appends a disclaimer whenever pred(y) != pred(y'), which is a noisy signal (predictions can differ due to sampling stochasticity rather than cue reliance); only one sampled counterfactual response is used, and no variance reduction or thresholding is explored.

The intervention operates by appending a fixed disclaimer to the RM input during training, which raises circularity concerns: the DPO model could learn to satisfy the RM by rephrasing rather than genuinely reducing cue reliance, and the eval LLM's acknowledgment detection may not distinguish these; the paper does not directly test whether protected-feature reliance itself is reduced (rather than just acknowledgment wording changing).

Limited comparison to alternative or stronger baselines: no direct empirical comparison with Turpin et al. (2025) pre-alignment verbalization training (discussed only textually), no RLHF/PPO experiments (only BoN and RM-annotated DPO), and only two relatively small generator LLMs; scaling behavior of the approach is unknown.

The method requires pre-built counterfactual prompts (and hand-written disclaimers) per setting, which limits practical applicability to real alignment pipelines where cues may be subtle or unknown; the proposed automated pipeline is left to future work.

Evaluation of acknowledgments depends on an LLM judge with notably weaker quality on BiasQA (F1 0.75, false positives acknowledged), which introduces noise into the key acknowledgment-rate metric used for the main conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question at the intersection of CoT faithfulness and reward hacking: reward models cannot observe the generator's decision process, so they may incentivize explanations tailored to the reward rather than to the actual reasoning.
The experimental design is careful and controlled: two distinct settings (Math Book, BiasQA), two reward models, two LLM generators, both BoN and DPO, with seeds and standard deviations reported.

Useful diagnostic evidence is provided (Figure 1b, B.1): reward models penalize responses that acknowledge the protected feature even when the answer is correct, empirically establishing the incentive structure for CoT hacking.

The RM_ALL ablation (Figure 7) is a good control showing that the benefit does not come merely from the semantic effect of appending disclaimers, and the appendix contains extensive supporting material including Eval LLM validation and a preliminary generalization experiment on CodeMMLU.
weaknesses: Limited generality: the method requires knowing the protected feature in advance and constructing instance-level counterfactual prompts, an oracle-like requirement acknowledged only as a limitation. Real reward-hacking scenarios rarely have such clean, known cues, so practical applicability is unclear.

The intervention itself is very simple: appending a hand-written template disclaimer to the RM input when a counterfactual prediction differs. The conceptual contribution (feed causal-attribution signals to the RM) is largely incremental over existing counterfactual faithfulness methodology (Turpin et al. 2023, Lanham et al. 2023, Matton et al. 2025, and the authors' own cited parallel work Turpin et al. 2025).

Effect sizes are modest and inconsistent. In DPO on 'Math Book', RMC reduces the gap by only 2.4 percentage points and RMD largely fails; improvements are stronger in BiasQA/BoN but uneven across RMs, LLMs, and decoding schemes, weakening the central claim that the approach reliably reduces CoT hacking.

There is a conceptual tension in the evaluation: the intervention works by penalizing responses whose predictions change under counterfactual removal of the cue, which necessarily drives accuracy toward the no-cue performance. The paper frames this purely as a win (less hacking), but the resulting accuracy loss is never discussed as a cost/trade-off, and the extent to which 'hacking reduction' is just 'accuracy suppression' is not disentangled.

The unfaithfulness metric and the intervention share the same counterfactual signal, creating a potential circularity: the method is optimized against, and evaluated with, essentially the same detection criterion.
Acknowledgment detection relies on an Eval LLM with weak performance on BiasQA (F1 = 0.75, tendency to false positives), adding noise to a key reported metric.

Only two synthetic controlled settings with small test sets (254 and 315 examples); the CodeMMLU generalization test is preliminary (single 300-example sample, small and mixed effects) and does not establish broader applicability.

Given the simplicity of the core idea, the paper would benefit from more analysis (e.g., how signal noise in counterfactual predictions affects results, sensitivity to disclaimer wording, comparison against simpler baselines such as response filtering) to justify a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important and timely problem ('CoT hacking'): reward models operating only on generated text cannot verify CoT faithfulness, and this creates concrete incentives for reward hacking during preference optimization. The motivation experiment (Figures 1b, 6) convincingly shows that off-the-shelf reward models penalize acknowledged use of protected features while rewarding unacknowledged use.

The proposed counterfactual-augmented reward model is simple, well-motivated, and computationally cheap (no RM retraining; only extra decoding of counterfactual prompts), and the paper transparently contrasts two signal strategies (RMD requiring no labels vs. RMC using cue alignment), with a sensible discussion of their trade-offs.

Evaluation is notably thorough for a controlled study: two complementary settings (Math Book, BiasQA), two LLM generators, two off-the-shelf RMs, two reward-guiding mechanisms (BoN and DPO), repeated runs with standard deviations, a Majority@N protocol, an ablation (RM_ALL) ruling out the trivial 'disclaimer semantics' explanation, a fine-grained unfaithfulness metric (Table 1), Eval LLM detection validated against manual annotation (F1 0.93/0.75), and a preliminary out-of-domain generalization test on CodeMMLU.

The paper is honest about limitations: results are presented with both strengths and failures (e.g., RMD 'mostly failing' on Math Book under DPO), and the conclusion explicitly discusses the restricted scope and the counterfactual-generation bottleneck.
weaknesses: Scope of empirical validation is narrow: two synthetic, hand-constructed settings where the protected feature is deliberately planted and easily removable. Real-world reward hacking involves diffuse, hard-to-isolate cues; the paper acknowledges but does not demonstrate generality, and the CodeMMLU generalization test is small, preliminary, and shows weak/mixed effects.

The mitigation effect is partial and inconsistent: for Math Book under DPO, RMC reduces the gap by only ~2.4 points and RMD largely fails; acknowledgment rates remain near zero in many configurations. The method suppresses cue exploitation in the RM's ranking rather than teaching the model to be faithful, so behavior could re-emerge or be gamed (e.g., a policy that generates responses whose counterfactual predictions coincide, evading the signal) - this evasion threat is not analyzed.

The 'interpretability signal' is a fixed, hand-written disclaimer string rather than a learned or general attribution; effectiveness likely depends on the RM's sensitivity to that exact text, and there is no analysis of robustness across RM families, prompt phrasings, or against adaptive policies.

Novelty is moderate: the counterfactual probing methodology is borrowed from prior faithfulness work (Turpin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025), and parallel work (Turpin et al., 2025) addresses the same cue-acknowledgment problem at a different stage of training; the main novel element is feeding the signal into the RM input, which is a fairly straightforward intervention.

Reliance on an Eval LLM (Llama-3.3-70B) for acknowledgment detection introduces measurement noise, particularly for BiasQA (F1 0.75), which directly affects headline metrics such as acknowledgment and unfaithfulness rates.
